She complains of an irritating, non-painful sensation in her legs that give her an overwhelming urge to move them. The symptoms occur when she is resting, and get worse from evening onwards. She does not take psychotropic medication, and a recent full blood count shows anaemia. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation:
Restless leg syndrome (Ekbom’s syndrome) is an irresistible desire to move the legs when resting with unpleasant leg sensations. It is usually idiopathic. Secondary causes include iron deficiency, uraemia, pregnancy, diabetes, polyneuropathy and rheumatoid arthritis. Dopamine agonists and benzodiazepines such as clonazepam are commonly used for treatment. In psychiatry, Ekbom’s syndrome also refers to delusional parasitosis.
Reference: Longmore M, Wilkinson I, Turmezei T, Cheung CK (2007). Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine (7th edition). Oxford, UK: Oxford University Press.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old woman presents with auditory hallucination, delusional perception and thought interferences. Psychiatric evaluation established a diagnosis of schizophrenia. She has a history of asthma. She started treatment with haloperidol 10 mg per day because she cannot afford second-generation antipsychotics and cannot tolerate chlorpromazine. Shortly after taking haloperidol, she felt restless with inner tension. Later, her mother reports that she frequently is unable to remain seated, shifts in place and shuffles from foot to foot. The following are appropriate treatments that you might try in order to relieve her symptoms except

options.text: Start her on an antimuscarinic drug

questions.explanation:
She suffers from akathisia. Options (A), (C), (D) and (E) are recommended for the treatment of antipsychotic-induced akathisia. Propranolol is contraindicated in patients with asthma. Cyproheptadine is not indicated.
Reference: Taylor D, Paton C, Kapur S (2009). The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (10th edition). London: Informa Healthcare.

questions.question_text: The sister of a man with schizophrenia has read about ‘simple schizophrenia’. Which of the following symptoms found in her brother do not support a diagnosis of simple schizophrenia?

options.text: Odd behaviour such as locking himself in the toilet and colouring the water in a bath tub

questions.explanation:
Florid third-person auditory hallucinations do not support the diagnosis of simple schizophrenia. Simple schizophrenia is characterized by negative symptoms with an insidious onset of decline in functioning and absence of prominent positive symptoms.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 593–609.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man complains that he hears voices from his late mother. Three months ago, his mother died in a car accident when he was driving his car. He feels very sad and guilty. He has not driven the car since the accident and he wants to sell the car. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
He suffers from a normal grief reaction. Sadness, guilt and transient experience of hearing voices of the deceased are common among people with normal grief reaction. The accident occurred 3 months ago, and there is no evidence of prolonged grief. There is not enough clinical evidence to suggest that he suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 811–817.

questions.question_text: A patient is on treatment with psychotropic medications. He wonders which of the following would affect his medications, by acting as an enzyme inducer:
questions.explanation:
Smoking is likely to affect the levels of his medication, as smoking would cause an induction of CYP1A2. This is due to the polycyclic hydrocarbons present in tobacco smoke. This enzyme is responsible for the metabolism of many common psychotropic drugs. Hence, smoking could reduce blood levels of drugs such as clozapine, haloperidol, chlorpromazine, olanzapine, tricyclic antidepressants, mirtazapine, fluvoxamine and propranolol by up to 50%.
Reference: Taylor D, Paton C, Kapur S (2009). The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (10th edition). London: Informa Healthcare, p. 506.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man complains of chest pain after his late father died of myocardial infarction 6 months ago. His wife feels that he has become very angry and hostile to her after his father passed away. He has been drinking heavily in the last 3 months. When you ask him the reason of heavy drinking, he wants to be self-destructive. Which of the following abnormal grief reactions is the most accurate diagnosis for this man?
questions.explanation:
Distorted grief is associated with intense anger or guilt. The person may develop symptoms that the deceased had prior to death. Other signs of distorted grief are over-activity without a sense of loss, hostility towards a specific person and taking self-destructive actions. Since the duration is only 6 months, he does not qualify for chronic grief. Conflicted grief refers to ambivalent feelings. Delayed grief refers to a bereaved person who does not show any grief reaction immediately. Inhibited grief refers to unexpressed grief feelings.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 811–817.

questions.question_text: Disorders of self-awareness (ego disorders) usually include the following disturbances except
questions.explanation:
Disorders of self-awareness include disturbances of awareness of self-activity, immediate awareness of self-unity, continuity of self and boundaries of self. Disorders of self-awareness include depersonalization (feeling altered or not real) and derealization (surroundings not appearing real).
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 9.

questions.question_text: You are teaching depressive disorder to a group of medical students. They want to know the percentage of patients admitted to the university hospital who will have recurrence and require further admission in the long run without committing suicide. Your answer is
questions.explanation:
An old British study showed that approximately 60% of patients had been re-admitted at least once. Only 20% had recovered fully with no further episodes and 20% were incapacitated throughout or died of suicide.
Reference: Lee AS, Murray RM (1988). The long-term outcome of Maudsley depressives. Br J Psychiatry, 153: 741–751.

questions.question_text: During an experiment, participants were asked to listen to a speech made by a speaker that supported or opposed World War II. Participants were told that the speech they were about to hear was chosen at random by tossing a coin. After listening to the speech, the participants were asked whether they thought the speaker believed in what he or she said about the war. The results showed that the participants thought the speaker believed in what he or she said even when they knew the positions were chosen at random. Which heuristic best explains the aforementioned phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
In this experiment, participants knew that the speaker’s position on the war was chosen at random, yet they thought the speaker believed in what he or she said. This is known as fundamental attribution error, defined as the tendency to overestimate the extent to which a person’s behaviour is due to internal, dispositional factors and to underestimate the role of external, situational factors. The anchoring and adjustment heuristic explains this phenomenon: participants use the speech as an initial 'anchor' to base their inference of the speaker’s disposition, then insufficiently adjust for situational factors.
Further Reading: Jones EE, Harris VA (1967). The attribution of attitudes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 3: 1–24.

questions.question_text: A new psychiatric consultant has been appointed by the trust to head a community psychiatric team. He is known to be a ‘hands-off’ person and not available most of the time. He seldom gives feedback to his team members. Which of the following teams will be effective under his leadership?

options.text: Assertive team members who request major decisions to be made by voting and thorough discussion amongst the whole team.
Team members who are eager to learn and request constant supervision from the consultant psychiatrist.
Honest team members who are good at performing routine home visits repeatedly.
Humble team members who prefer the consultant psychiatrist to make major decisions.
Trustworthy team members who are experienced in community psychiatry and skilful in dealing with complicated issues. They require minimal supervision.

correct_answer.text: Trustworthy team members who are experienced in community psychiatry and skilful in dealing with complicated issues. They require minimal supervision.

correct_answers.text: Trustworthy team members who are experienced in community psychiatry and skilful in dealing with complicated issues. They require minimal supervision.

questions.explanation:
This case refers to laissez-faire leadership. Trustworthy team members who are experienced and require minimal supervision will work best under a ‘hands-off’ leader.
Further Reading: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 292, 118.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old woman is admitted due to elated mood. A core trainee wants to know the differences between hypomania and mania. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: Patients with hypomania are not expected to have hallucinations.
Patients with hypomania are not expected to have mood-congruent delusions.
Patients with mania are expected to have reckless behaviour.
Patients with mania and hypomania are expected to have elated mood.
Patients with mania and hypomania are expected to have the same level of psychosocial functioning.

correct_answer.text: Patients with mania and hypomania are expected to have the same level of psychosocial functioning.

correct_answers.text: Patients with mania and hypomania are expected to have the same level of psychosocial functioning.

questions.explanation:
Patients with mania have a lower level of psychosocial functioning compared with patients with hypomania.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 610, 624–627.

questions.question_text: A 33-year-old female has been diagnosed with PTSD after having witnessed a gun-shot incident in the supermarket that she was shopping at. She wants to get well as soon as possible and is keen on both pharmacological and psychological therapy. From your knowledge about PTSD management, which of the following would be contraindicated in her case?
questions.explanation:
Based on the NICE guidelines, debriefing is contraindicated for the management of PTSD. Trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, exposure therapy and social support are indicated.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 424.

questions.question_text: A trainee passes the MRCPsych examination Paper 1 having based her revision on past examination questions but other trainees who have studied for long hours and based their revision on textbooks failed Paper 1 despite having gained vast knowledge. The phenomenon being described is
questions.explanation:
Practice effect is the influence of test-taking performance due to prior exposure to a test, usually resulting in improved scores. Barnum effect is the tendency of people to endorse vague descriptions as accurately describing themselves. Halo effect is the influence of a positive or negative first impression on subsequent interpretations. Primacy and recency effects refer to remembering information at the start or end more accurately than the middle.
References: Collie A, Maruff P, Darby DG, McStephen M (2003). The effects of practice on the cognitive test performance of neurologically normal individuals assessed at brief test-retest intervals. Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society, 9: 419–428; Claridge G, Clark K, Powney E, Hassan E (2008). Schizotypy and the Barnum effect. Personality and Individual Differences, 44: 436–444; Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, p. 251.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman is a known case of schizophrenia. She presented to the Accident and Emergency Department with altered mental status, severe stiffness along with rapid eye blinking, unusual head and neck movements, and peculiar behaviour (simulating the doctor’s movement). She is afebrile, and creatinine kinase is normal. Which of the following signs is not associated with her condition?
questions.explanation:
She has catatonia. Clinical features of catatonia include stupor, posturing, negativism, stereotypy, mannerism, echolalia, echopraxia, automatic obedience and gegenhalten. Astasia-abasia is a gait disturbance seen in conversion disorder.
Reference: Rajagopal S (2007). Catatonia. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment, 13: 51–59.

questions.question_text: The following is a condition that is common in Southeast Asia and China. A Chinese man has extreme anxiety and fear of impending death due to worries that his genitals might retract into his abdomen and would disappear. This condition is known as
questions.explanation:
This condition is known as Koro. It may occur in epidemic form. It involves the belief of genital retraction with disappearance into the abdomen and is accompanied by intense anxiety and fear of impending death. The development of Koro has been associated with psychosexual conflicts, personality factors and cultural beliefs in the context of psychological stress.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 462.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old pregnant woman develops depression during the second trimester. Which of the following symptoms is the least reliable in establishing the diagnosis of depression?

options.text: Lack of interest in the baby

questions.explanation:
Somatic symptoms of depression (e.g. sleep, appetite, energy and libido changes) are not reliable in establishing the diagnosis of depression in the antenatal period because non-depressed pregnant women also experience insomnia, poor appetite, nausea, tiredness and libido changes.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 715–732.

questions.question_text: A core trainee has determined that the patient he interviewed has moderate depression and would benefit from an antidepressant. The other medical problems the patient has include that of hypertension and seizure. The core trainee wonders which antidepressant he should avoid, as it might affect his seizure threshold. Which of the following medications should be avoided?
questions.explanation:
Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure disorder because it lowers the seizure threshold. Most tricyclic antidepressants are also epileptogenic, particularly at higher doses. If antidepressant treatment is necessary, moclobemide and SSRIs are good choices. Mirtazapine, venlafaxine and duloxetine require extra care.
Reference: Taylor D, Paton C, Kapur S (2009). The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (10th edition). London: Informa Healthcare, p. 421.

questions.question_text: Based on the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale, which of the following events is considered to be the most stressful event contributing to illness?

options.text: Death of a close family member

questions.explanation:
Death of a spouse is considered to be the most stressful event with 100 life change units (LCU), followed by divorce (73 LCU), marital separation (65 LCU), imprisonment (63 LCU) and death of a close family member (63 LCU).
Reference: Holmes TH, Rahe RH (1967). The Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 11: 213–218; Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 155–156.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted to the psychiatric ward. The nurse informs you that he lies for hours on his bed with his head raised 10 cm off the mattress. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation:
Psychological pillow is a feature of catatonia. The patient holds his or her head a few inches above the bed surface in a reclining posture and is able to maintain this position for hours.
Reference: Rajagopal S (2007). Catatonia. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment, 13: 51–59.

questions.question_text: In an animal experiment, a rat pressed a lever in the cage and got an electric shock. The rat has never pressed the lever again ever since it was nearly electrocuted. The phenomenon being described is
questions.explanation:
This phenomenon is punishment because it results in a reduction in behaviour. Punishment is any stimulus that is applied after a response and causes a weakening of that behaviour. Punishment is the opposite of reinforcement (both positive and negative). Reinforcement causes a strengthening of the behaviour, whereas punishment suppresses it.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 200–205.

questions.question_text: The Nuremberg Code, which was formulated in 1947, is a very important piece of documentation regarding the ethics of medical research. Which of the following statements pertaining to the code is incorrect?

options.text: The trial involved conducting inquiries about doctors in wartime who performed human experiments in concentration camps.
The trial involved Japanese doctors who were deemed unethical.
The trial involved Nazi doctors who were deemed unethical.
As a result of the trial, this led to a set of 10 research principles.
The trial led to doctors recognizing the need to respect the human rights of subjects.

correct_answer.text: The trial involved Japanese doctors who were deemed unethical.

correct_answers.text: The trial involved Japanese doctors who were deemed unethical.

questions.explanation:
The Nuremberg Code arose from the trial of Nazi doctors who performed unethical human experiments in concentration camps. It did not involve Japanese doctors. The trial led to a set of 10 research principles and recognition of subjects’ rights.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 147.

questions.question_text: In an animal experiment, a rat will get food after it presses a lever. The learning process being described is
questions.explanation:
Operant conditioning involves learning of voluntary behaviour through the effects of its consequences (e.g. a rat pressing a lever to obtain food).
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 200–205.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be used to prevent groupthink?
questions.explanation:
Assigning each member the role of a critical evaluator helps prevent groupthink by encouraging dissent and examination of alternatives.
Reference: Aronson E, Wilson TD, Akert RM (2007). Social Psychology. Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall, pp. 160–162.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male, Jordan, came to the emergency department, requesting to see Sarah, the psychiatric nurse who treated him 3 weeks ago. He is demanding to see her as he believes that she is in love with him, just from the way she smiled at him previously when he was undergoing treatment. He is keen to take her out for a date and engage in sexual acts with her. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Erotomania is a delusional disorder in which the patient believes that another person, often of higher status, is in love with him or her.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 6.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man suffers from chronic schizophrenia. Three months ago, he developed shortness of breath, numbness, difficulty in handling tools and trouble in walking down the stairs. He came to the Accident and Emergency Department a few times, and the doctors felt that he presented with somatic complaints and then discharged him. His GP urged the doctors at the Accident and Emergency Department to admit this man for further evaluation. He turned out to suffer from cervical cord compression and required urgent operation. After the operation, he developed tetraplegia. His wife is very upset with the hospital. When the Chief Executive meets his wife, he says, ‘It is quite acceptable to feel angry at the hospital and perhaps most people would feel angry as you do’. The Chief Executive demonstrates which of the following techniques?
questions.explanation:
Legitimation involves validating the patient's or relative’s feelings—acknowledging that anger is acceptable and understood.
Reference: Poole R, Higgo R (2006). Psychiatric Interviewing and Assessment. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press.

questions.question_text: A 29-year-old female has been diagnosed with rapid cycling bipolar disorder, as she has had more than four mood episodes per year. She is currently on pharmacological treatment with valproate. Which of the following factors might have an impact on her condition?
questions.explanation:
Rapid cycling in bipolar disorder is often induced by antidepressant use. Other exacerbating factors include thyroid dysfunction and substance use.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 397.

questions.question_text: A common cultural-bound syndrome described in North America, in which individuals believe that he or she might have undergone a transformation and become a monster that would practise cannibalism is known as
questions.explanation:
Windigo is a culturally bound syndrome among some North American indigenous peoples involving a delusional belief of becoming a cannibalistic monster.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 463.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following terminologies best describes the ratio between the minimum plasma level that would cause a toxic effect and the minimum plasma level that would cause therapeutic effects?
questions.explanation:
Therapeutic index is defined as the ratio of the median toxic dose to the median effective dose; it measures a drug’s safety margin.
Reference: Sadock BJ, Sadock VA (2008). Kaplan and Sadock’s Concise Textbook of Psychiatry (3rd edition). Philadelphia, PA: Lippincott, Williams & Wilkins, p. 915.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman meets the diagnostic criteria for panic disorder with agoraphobia. Each time she leaves the house, she experiences high levels of anxiety. When she goes back home, her anxiety level goes down. After some time, she learns that by staying at home, she can avoid any possibility of a panic attack in public. This contributes to the maintenance of her disorder. Which of the following statements about the aforementioned phenomenon is incorrect?

options.text: The reinforcement is contingent upon the behaviour.
A negative reinforcer positively affects the frequency of response.
The reinforcement can occur before the behaviour.
An alteration in the frequency of behaviour is possible after reinforcement.

correct_answer.text: The reinforcement can occur before the behaviour.

correct_answers.text: The reinforcement can occur before the behaviour.

questions.explanation:
In operant conditioning, reinforcement (relief from anxiety) occurs only after the behaviour (staying home). It does not occur before the behaviour.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 200–205.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with agoraphobia. She attends psychotherapy sessions for the treatment of her agoraphobia. Which of the following statements about the aforementioned phenomenon is incorrect?

options.text: Spontaneous recovery can occur after extinction.
Intermittent reinforcement diminishes the extinction rate.
Implosion cannot be used in extinction.
Reciprocal inhibition can be used in extinction.

correct_answer.text: Implosion cannot be used in extinction.

correct_answers.text: Implosion cannot be used in extinction.

questions.explanation:
Implosion (imaginal flooding) can be used in extinction. It involves intense imagined exposure to the feared stimulus. It is not excluded from extinction techniques.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 199, 990–991.

questions.question_text: Which of the following concepts do not contribute to the aetiology of phobias?
questions.explanation:
Learned helplessness is not implicated in phobia aetiology. Phobias arise via classical conditioning, are maintained by avoidance (Mowrer’s two-factor theory), can be acquired vicariously and reflect evolutionary preparedness.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 195–200.

questions.question_text: Eugen Bleuler proposed the term ‘schizophrenia’ for what Emil Kraepelin had been calling ‘dementia praecox’. The reason was

options.text: The term ‘schizophrenia’ refers to a disorder with onset in young adulthood that is different from dementia, which usually occurs in old age.
The term ‘schizophrenia’ refers to a chronic disorder comprising hallucinations and delusions with a downhill course.
The term ‘schizophrenia’ refers to the integration of functional psychiatric disorder and organic disorder (e.g. catatonia).
The term ‘schizophrenia’ refers to a significant deterioration of social functioning and poor long-term outcome that occurred in the era of asylums.
The term ‘schizophrenia’ refers to the ‘splitting’ of affect from other psychological functions leading to a dissociation between the social situation and the emotion expressed.

correct_answer.text: The term ‘schizophrenia’ refers to the ‘splitting’ of affect from other psychological functions leading to a dissociation between the social situation and the emotion expressed.

correct_answers.text: The term ‘schizophrenia’ refers to the ‘splitting’ of affect from other psychological functions leading to a dissociation between the social situation and the emotion expressed.

questions.explanation:
Bleuler chose ‘schizophrenia’ (literally ‘split mind’) to reflect the splitting of affect from other mental functions, rather than early dementia.
References: Charlton B (2000). Psychiatry and the Human Condition. Oxford, UK: Radcliffe Publishing; Shorter E (1997). A History of Psychiatry. New York: John Wiley & Sons.

questions.question_text: During a routine physical examination for extra-pyramidal side effects, it was noted that the patient kept stretching out his hands, withdrawing them thereafter and repeating this several times, without allowing the examiner to check for the presence of Parkinson’s features in the upper limbs. This form of psychopathology is termed as
questions.explanation:
Ambitendency involves making repeated tentative, incomplete movements (e.g. reaching out then withdrawing the hand repeatedly).
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 1.

questions.question_text: In the United Kingdom, the determinants of social class are based on
questions.explanation:
UK social class is traditionally determined by occupation categories (e.g. professional, managerial, skilled, unskilled).
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 115.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male was involved in a road traffic accident. When he awoke post-surgery, he realized that he is unable to recall events leading up to the accident.
questions.explanation:
Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memory for events that occurred before the precipitating incident.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 103.

questions.question_text: An MMSE assessment was conducted for a 70-year-old man. He was noted to be unable to recall the three items to which he was presented with.
questions.explanation:
Inability to recall three memorized items after an interval reflects impairment of working (short-term) memory.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 103.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old female with dementia is still able to remember how to sew her dresses as she has been a tailor previously when she was younger.
questions.explanation:
Procedural memory (implicit memory) for learned skills (e.g. sewing) often remains intact in dementia.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 103.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old male was asked to name the capital of the United Kingdom. Which type of memory is he using?
questions.explanation:
Naming facts (e.g. capital city) uses declarative (semantic) memory, a subset of explicit memory.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 103.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old female has Alzheimer’s dementia, but she is still able to remember personal events that happened when she was much younger and is still able to share her life story with her grandchildren. Which form of memory is she relying on?
questions.explanation:
Recollection of personal past events uses episodic memory (a subset of declarative memory).
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 103.

questions.question_text: Amphetamines: approximate duration that they could still be detected in the urine.
questions.explanation:
Amphetamines can usually be detected in urine for about 48 hours after use.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 529.

questions.question_text: Barbiturates: approximate duration that they could still be detected in the urine.
questions.explanation:
Short-acting barbiturates are detectable for about 24 hours in urine (long-acting barbiturates may be detectable for longer).
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 529.

questions.question_text: Cocaine: approximate duration that it could still be detected in the urine.
questions.explanation:
Cocaine metabolites are typically detectable in urine for about 6–8 hours after use.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 529.

questions.question_text: Heroin: approximate duration that it could still be detected in the urine.
questions.explanation:
Heroin (morphine) metabolites are detectable in urine for approximately 36–72 hours.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 529.

questions.question_text: Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD): approximate duration that it could still be detected in the urine.
questions.explanation:
LSD is generally detectable in urine for about 12–24 hours after ingestion.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 529.

questions.question_text: Methylene-dioxy-methamphetamine (MDMA): approximate duration that it could still be detected in the urine.
questions.explanation:
MDMA can usually be detected in urine for around 48 hours after use.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 529.

questions.question_text: Phencyclidine (PCP): approximate duration that it could still be detected in the urine.
questions.explanation:
PCP metabolites can be detected in urine for up to 8 days after use.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 529.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia for his child if his wife also suffers from schizophrenia. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation:
If both parents have schizophrenia, the risk for the child is approximately 46%, which falls in the 35%–50% range.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 474–475.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia for his child if his wife does not suffer from schizophrenia. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation:
With one affected parent, the risk for the child is about 13%, corresponding to 10%–14%.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 474–475.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia if he adopted a child with velocardiofacial syndrome. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation:
Velocardiofacial syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) carries about a 23% risk of schizophrenia.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 597, 599.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his half-siblings. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation:
Half-siblings share about 25% of genes; the risk is around 2%–4%, consistent with 0%–4%.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 474–475.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his younger cousin. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation:
A first cousin has about a 2.4% risk—so falls in the 0%–4% range.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 474–475.

questions.question_text: A 10-year-old boy develops obsessions and compulsive behaviour after a sore throat and fever. (Choose one option.)

options.text: Death of the mother before the age of 11 years
Three children at home under the age of 14 years

questions.explanation:
PANDAS (pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections) presents with OCD symptoms following a strep throat.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, p. 551.

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old woman presents with recurrent self-harm following the end of a transient and intense romantic relationship. She has a chronic feeling of emptiness and exhibits binge-eating behaviour. (Choose one option.)

options.text: Death of the mother before the age of 11 years
Three children at home under the age of 14 years

questions.explanation:
Childhood sexual abuse is a known etiological factor in borderline personality disorder, which presents with self-harm, chronic emptiness and impulsive behaviors.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 707, 709.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man complains that MI5 is monitoring him and has tried to control his feelings and intentions. He hears the voices of two secret agents talking about him and they issue him with a command. (Choose three options.)

options.text: Death of the mother before the age of 11 years
Three children at home under the age of 14 years

questions.explanation:
Schizophrenia is associated with multiple genetic risk factors (e.g. dysbindin and neuregulin genes) and with migration. These three etiological factors apply to his paranoid and passivity symptoms.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 593–609.

questions.question_text: A nurse was involved in a road traffic accident recently, about 3 months ago. Since then, she has been experiencing nightmares, flashbacks as well as irritable mood.
questions.explanation:
PTSD arises within 6 months of an exceptionally threatening event, with flashbacks, nightmares and hyperarousal.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 427.

questions.question_text: A 21-year-old male has been recently enrolled into the military service and he has persistent low mood associated with loss of interest. He finds himself having much difficulty with coping with the demands of the military.
questions.explanation:
Adjustment disorder occurs within one month of an identifiable stressor and causes emotional or behavioral symptoms out of proportion to the stress.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 432.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old female finds that over the past 6 months she has been increasingly worried about everyday little things.
questions.explanation:
Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by excessive worry about multiple everyday events for at least 6 months.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 409.

questions.question_text: Patients with this condition usually present with the disease during adolescence; however, the clinical onset may be detected as cognitive impairment, abnormal behaviour and personality change, and renal, haematological and endocrine symptoms.

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone hyper-secretion

questions.explanation:
Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism, presenting in adolescence with neuropsychiatric, hepatic, renal and endocrine symptoms.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 477.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female is no longer able to meet the demands of her job as she has been complaining of excessive tiredness, lethargy as well as constipation. She has no previous known medical history and has not been on long-term medications.

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone hyper-secretion

questions.explanation:
Hypothyroidism is common in middle-aged women and presents with fatigue, lethargy and constipation. Treatment with thyroxine often reverses psychiatric symptoms.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 477.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old female has been feeling edgy quite recently and complaining that she has lost a huge amount of weight despite her good appetite.

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone hyper-secretion

questions.explanation:
Hyperthyroidism causes anxiety, weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance and tremor.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 480.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old female has long-standing irregular menses, and now presents with gradually worsening hirsutism and weight gain. She also has been having acne on her face and feeling depressed.

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone hyper-secretion

questions.explanation:
Cushing’s syndrome presents with weight gain, central obesity, irregular menses, hirsutism, acne and mood changes due to cortisol excess.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 482.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old female presents with weakness, dizziness, anorexia, weight loss and gastrointestinal disturbance. On physical examination, there is noted to be generalized hyper-pigmentation of the skin and mucous membrane. She also has postural hypotension and loss of pubic hairs.

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone hyper-secretion

questions.explanation:
Addison’s disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) presents with hyperpigmentation, weight loss, anorexia, postural hypotension and loss of secondary sexual hair.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 483.

questions.question_text: Based on the ICD-10, this is the most common subtype in which hallucinations and/or delusions are prominent.
questions.explanation:
Paranoid schizophrenia is the most common subtype, characterized by prominent delusions and auditory hallucinations.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 353.

questions.question_text: Based on the ICD-10, the age of onset of this condition is between 15 and 25 years. This particular subtype has been known to be associated with a poor prognosis.
questions.explanation:
Hebephrenic (disorganized) schizophrenia has onset typically at 15–25 years and carries a poorer prognosis with prominent affective disturbances.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 353.

questions.question_text: Based on the ICD-10 classification system, in this particular form of schizophrenia, psychomotor disturbances may alternate between extremes and violent excitement may occur.
questions.explanation:
Catatonic schizophrenia features psychomotor disturbances including stupor, excitement, rigidity, posturing and violent excitement.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 353.

questions.question_text: Based on the ICD-10 classification system, for individuals with this condition, there is an insidious onset of decline in functioning.
questions.explanation:
Simple schizophrenia has an insidious onset of negative symptoms and decline in functioning without prior florid positive symptoms.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 353.

questions.question_text: In order to make this diagnosis, there must be the absence of depression, institutionalization or dementia or other brain disorders.
questions.explanation:
Residual schizophrenia requires a past history of schizophrenia and now only negative symptoms remain, with no active positive symptoms and no depression, dementia or organic brain disorder.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 354.

questions.question_text: For schizophrenia, the heritability estimate is around this value.
questions.explanation:
Twin and family studies estimate schizophrenia heritability at approximately 80%–85%.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 290.

questions.question_text: For depressive disorder, the heritability estimate is around this value.
questions.explanation:
Heritability estimates for major depression are around 40% based on twin studies.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 290.

questions.question_text: For bipolar disorder, the heritability estimate is around this value.
questions.explanation:
Bipolar disorder shows very high heritability, estimated around 79%–93% (approximately 80%).
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 290.

questions.question_text: For panic disorders, the heritability estimate is around this value.
questions.explanation: Based on key studies (Kendler et al., 1992), the estimates are around 44%

questions.question_text: In individuals with narcolepsy, this refers to the temporary loss of muscle tone.
questions.explanation: Cataplexy refers to the sudden, temporary loss of muscle tone seen in narcolepsy.

questions.question_text: Patients with this psychopathology would make a series of tentative incomplete movements when expected to carry out a voluntary action.
questions.explanation: Ambitendency is characterized by repeated, tentative, incomplete movements when attempting a voluntary action.

questions.question_text: Patients with this psychopathology would maintain abnormal postures.
questions.explanation: Catalepsy refers to the maintenance of rigid or unusual postures for prolonged periods.

questions.question_text: Individuals with this psychopathology embark on a series of behaviours when they are asleep.
questions.explanation: Somnambulism (sleepwalking) involves complex behaviours performed while asleep.

questions.question_text: This form of psychopathology is commonly referred to as the motor component of an obsessive thought.
questions.explanation: Compulsions are the repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to neutralize or reduce anxiety associated with an obsession.

questions.question_text: This form of psychopathology commonly refers to repeated doubts and compulsive rituals.
questions.explanation: Obsessional slowness refers to the slowed behaviour and frequent rituals caused by repeated doubts and compulsions.

questions.question_text: This form of psychopathology might be seen in catatonic states, depressive states or even manic states.
questions.explanation: Stupor is a state of diminished responsiveness and motor activity seen in catatonia, severe depression or mania.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male has just undergone six cycles of electroconvulsive therapy. He claimed to be having problems with his memories – forming new memories as well as recalling old memories. Which terminology correctly describes the pathology that James is experiencing?
questions.explanation: James has both anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) and retrograde amnesia (loss of past memories) following ECT.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old male has just been involved in a major car accident. He lost consciousness immediately after the collision. He finds himself having major difficulties recollecting what has happened. Which terminology correctly describes the pathology that Tom is experiencing?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic amnesia is the time after a head injury during which the patient cannot recall events, reflecting the period of disorientation.

questions.question_text: A medical student was clerking a psychiatric inpatient, John. He realized that John was unable to recollect his own personal information, but appeared unconcerned about his memory loss. Which terminology best describes this psychopathology?
questions.explanation: Psychogenic (dissociative) amnesia involves inability to recall personal information, often with la belle indifférence (lack of concern).

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old female’s family members brought her into the emergency services. They were concerned about her having a sudden onset of disorientation and being unable to recollect immediate events. Which terminology best describes this psychopathology?
questions.explanation: Transient global amnesia presents with sudden onset of anterograde and retrograde memory loss for a few hours, then resolves without recurrence.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old has been a chronic alcoholic. A medical student was assessing his memory and found that Thomas was confabulating at times. Which terminology best describes this psychopathology?
questions.explanation: Paramnesia refers to distorted recall and confabulation, filling gaps in memory with fabricated details.

questions.question_text: In this condition, the person may have difficulties with naming objects or arranging words in the right sequences. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Intermediate (conduction or nominal) aphasia involves difficulty in naming and word sequencing despite preserved comprehension.

questions.question_text: In this condition, the person may have difficulties with comprehending the meaning of words. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Receptive (Wernicke’s) aphasia is characterized by impaired comprehension of spoken or written words.

questions.question_text: In this condition, the person may have difficulties in expressing thoughts in words but comprehension is normal. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Expressive (Broca’s) aphasia involves effortful speech production with intact comprehension.

questions.question_text: In this condition, the person may have difficulties in expressing thoughts in words and also comprehending words. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Global aphasia is the most severe form, with marked impairment of both expression and comprehension.

questions.question_text: This refers to the gradual increment in the strength of the conditioned response.
questions.explanation: Incubation is the process by which conditioned responses become stronger over time.

questions.question_text: The process whereby a response initially evoked by one stimulus could now be evoked by stimuli similar to the original.
questions.explanation: Generalization occurs when a conditioned response is elicited by stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus.

questions.question_text: This refers to a process in which a conditioned stimulus is being paired with a second or third conditioned stimulus which, on presentation by itself, would elicit the original conditioned response.
questions.explanation: Higher-order conditioning involves pairing a new conditioned stimulus with an existing one so that the new stimulus eventually elicits the response.

questions.question_text: In this form of learning or conditioning, it has been noted that the learning and conditioning becomes less effective as the time interval between the two increases.
questions.explanation: Trace conditioning is less effective as the interval between conditioned and unconditioned stimuli increases.

questions.question_text: This process of learning is considered to be optimal when the delay between the onsets of the two stimuli is around half a second.
questions.explanation: Delayed conditioning, with the conditioned stimulus preceding and overlapping the unconditioned stimulus, is most effective when the delay is about 0.5 seconds.

questions.question_text: The failure to negotiate this stage leads to hysterical personality traits.
questions.explanation: Failure to negotiate the phallic stage (ages 3–6) can lead to hysterical and competitive personality traits.

questions.question_text: The failure to negotiate this stage leads to personality traits such as obsessive-compulsive personality, tidiness and rigidity.
questions.explanation: Failure to negotiate the anal stage (ages 1–3) can result in traits of obsessiveness, rigidity and orderliness.

questions.question_text: The failure to negotiate this stage might lead to generosity, depression and elation.
questions.explanation: Failure to negotiate the oral stage (birth–1 year) can result in mood swings, generosity or pessimism.

questions.question_text: Which of the aforementioned Erikson’s stages is a 5-year-old child undergoing?
questions.explanation: A 5-year-old child is in Erikson’s stage of initiative (ages 3–6), learning to plan and undertake tasks.

questions.question_text: Which of the aforementioned Erikson’s stages is a teenager undergoing?
questions.explanation: the stage that lasts from the age of 15 years to adulthood is that of intimacy

questions.question_text: This particular type of leadership is more appropriate for creative and open-ended tasks.
questions.explanation: Laissez-faire leadership works best when team members are skilled, independent, and tasks are creative or open-ended.

questions.question_text: For this particular type of leadership, there is a tendency for the tasks to be abandoned in the absence of the leader.
questions.explanation: Autocratic leaders make decisions themselves; in their absence, teams may stall or abandon tasks.

questions.question_text: This refers to the power derived from assignment to a specific role.
questions.explanation: Authority power comes from one’s formal position or role, granting the right to make decisions.

questions.question_text: This refers to the power derived from the ability to allocate resources.
questions.explanation: Reward power is based on the capacity to provide valued rewards or resources.

questions.question_text: This refers to the power derived from skill, knowledge and experience.
questions.explanation: Expert power arises from recognized expertise, skills or knowledge in a particular domain.

questions.question_text: Animism, in which life, thoughts and feelings are attributed to all objects, including inanimate ones, commonly develops during this stage.
questions.explanation: Animistic thinking is characteristic of Piaget’s preoperational stage (ages 2–7).

questions.question_text: Primary, secondary and tertiary circular reactions develop during this stage.
questions.explanation: Circular reactions (repeated actions) occur in the sensorimotor stage (birth–2 years).

questions.question_text: This is the stage that is characterized by the achievement of being able to think in the abstract.
questions.explanation: Formal operational stage (from ~12 years) is marked by abstract and hypothetical thinking.

questions.question_text: This is the stage in which an understanding of the laws of conservation, number and volume and then weight is normally achieved.
questions.explanation:
this is the third stage and occurs from the age of 7 to around 12–14
years of age. During this stage, the child demonstrates logical thought processes and
more subjective moral judgements. An understanding of the laws of conservation of,
initially, number and volume and the weight is normally achieved. Reversibility and
some aspects of classifications are mastered.

questions.question_text: This particular questionnaire is administered to a relative or friend who is asked to answer the questions on the basis of performance over the previous 6 months.
questions.explanation: The Blessed Dementia Scale is completed by an informant reporting on the patient’s function over the prior six months.

questions.question_text: This is an interview schedule that has three components: a structured clinical interview, a range of objective cognitive tests and a structured interview with a relative or informant.
questions.explanation: The Cambridge Examination for Mental Disorders (CAMDEX) includes patient interview, cognitive tests (CAMCOG) and informant interview.

questions.question_text: Amongst all of the options, this is considered to be a nursing-rated assessment.
questions.explanation: The Clifton Assessment Schedule is a nursing-rated tool for dementia evaluation.

questions.question_text: This particular questionnaire involves interviewing the carer more about the psychopathology associated with dementia.
questions.explanation: The Present Behavioural Examination focuses on interviewing carers about the patient’s behavioural changes in dementia.

questions.question_text: Which one of the aforementioned has the highest life change value based on the Holmes and Rahe (1967) life-change scale?

options.text: Death of a close family member

questions.explanation: Death of a spouse has the highest score of 100 on the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale.

questions.question_text: Which one of the aforementioned has the second highest life-change value based on the Holmes and Rahe (1967) life-change scale?

options.text: Death of a close family member

questions.explanation: Divorce carries the second-highest value at 73 life-change units.

questions.question_text: Which one of the aforementioned has a life-change value of approximately 50 based on the Holmes and Rahe (1967) life-change scale?

options.text: Death of a close family member

questions.explanation: Pregnancy has a life-change value of 50 on the Holmes and Rahe scale.

questions.question_text: Which one of the aforementioned has the lowest life-change value?

options.text: Death of a close family member

questions.explanation: Minor legal violation has the lowest score of 11 life-change units.
